title: Sequence diagrams for one use case
idea: A sequence diagram shows one scenario as messages between objects over time, so you can check who calls whom, in what order, and what comes back.
points: Objects sit across the top; time runs down each dashed lifeline.
Solid arrow with filled head is a call; dashed arrow is its return.
`alt` draws branches; `loop` repeats a block; `opt` runs only if true.
Draw it after the class diagram to find missing methods and wrong owners.

messages.label: placeOrder(sku, qty)
messages.note: The controller makes one call. `OrderService` is now active until it replies.

messages.label: reserve(sku, qty)
messages.note: The service coordinates. It holds stock first, so payment never charges for missing goods.

messages.label: reserved
messages.note: A dashed arrow is the return. Control is back with the caller.

messages.label: charge(cents)
messages.note: The service computes the amount itself. Each arrow is a method the receiver must own.

messages.label: approved
messages.note: The reply picks a branch. A decline would take the `else` path shown in the Mermaid code below.

messages.label: commit(sku, qty)
messages.note: Approved: the reservation becomes a sale. Declined would send `release` here instead.

messages.label: CONFIRMED
messages.note: The final return ends the activation. Read top to bottom, this is the method body.

code.title: The diagram
code.caption: Both paths in one Mermaid diagram, with an `alt` frame for the payment result.

walk.text: Each participant gets a lifeline. Order them left to right in the order they are first called.
`->>` is a call and `-->>` its return. `+` and `-` open and close activation bars.
The payment reply decides which branch below runs.
`alt` and `else` show mutually exclusive branches. Name each guard so readers know the condition.
Deactivate the service once it has replied in either branch.

code.title: The code behind it
code.caption: The service prints each outgoing call, so the run reproduces both branches of the diagram.

walk.text: First arrow from the service: reserve stock. It throws if stock is short.
The service computes the amount, then sends the `charge` message.
The `alt` approved branch: commit the reservation and return `CONFIRMED`.
The `else` branch: release the stock, or it leaks, then report the decline.
A fake gateway with a fixed limit keeps both paths deterministic.
The second order is declined, yet stock returns: free plus sold equals the start.

pitfalls: Drawing every getter call hides the flow; show messages that change state or cross objects.
Forgetting the failure branch; reviewers ask what happens when payment fails and stock stays held.
An arrow naming a method the receiver lacks means the class diagram is stale.

quiz.q: In the diagram, a dashed arrow with an open head goes from Inventory to OrderService. What is it?
options: The return of OrderService's earlier call
A dependency between the two classes
quiz.why: In sequence diagrams a dashed arrow is a reply to an earlier synchronous call. Asynchronous sends use a solid line with an open arrowhead.

takeaway: One scenario, top to bottom: every arrow must be a real method.

starters: How many sequence diagrams should I draw in an LLD interview?
How do I show an asynchronous event or a callback?
Should the controller or the service own the payment call?
